## 3. The three routes, priced from the notes

### Route A: keep the rule, flatten the tower

- Checker: nothing. The count goes 103 to 22, 82 errors gone (61 exclusion, 2 `comprises`, 19 in `RangeInternals` by a mechanism not traced) and 1 new; still masked at `FortressLibrary.fsi:2526` and never reaching the component (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 5`). The tripwire test `XXXExclusionRelaxRungP` is deleted in the same change (`REPORT.md`, "The three homes").
- Code generator: nothing this route requires; the two side defects stay.
- Library: 14 declaration headers (58 lines in the `.fsi`, 62 in the `.fss`, one in each `FortressBuiltin` file); `Number` gives up 52 api declarations and 57 bodies and `RR64` takes its own arithmetic on; 15 inherited methods restated on the leaves (24 method-leaf pairs); `SUM` and `PROD` rewritten, three options open; the `DistributesOver` markers dropped; `AnyIntegral comprises { ZZ, ... }` becomes well formed and the `NOT YET` accommodation of 2026-09-21 goes (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 1, § 6`).
- Interpreter: coercion called at dispatch and at typed bindings, 150-200 lines in six files, the compiled side's own mechanism (remedy i); or, without it, 160 library and 207 test sites converted by hand and the same in every future program (remedy ii). One line, `FortressLibrary.fss:4121`, is reached by every passing test, so the interpreter rung lands first (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 3, § 6`).
- The compiled side's precedent for remedy (i): of the 40 programs in `library_tests/`, 12 name a type wider than `ZZ32` and 9 bind an integer literal to one, every one through the prelude's `coerce`, none by hand (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 3`).
- Tests: under (i) no test text changes by design, but some outputs can: `x: ZZ64 = 2147483647; x + 1` wraps today because the value stays 32-bit; new coercion tests on both paths; one `typecase` site converted regardless (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 6`).
- Forecloses: the specification's `Empty extends List[\T\]` on the compiled path (any keep route does); ℤ as a subtype of ℚ, which becomes `RR64 coerce(x: ZZ)`; row 330's promotion by subtyping, which survives as static coercion on the compiled path and needs remedy (i) under walk, its unbounded half untouched; "any Number non-parametrically" (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 4`). Keeps the shortcut.
- Not settled: generic inference over mixed widths, where the flat join is `AnyIntegral` (`lo:hi`); whether the compiled checker coerces a functional method's `self`; 212 candidate lines no test runs; the component's type check; which `SUM` replacement (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 6`). And a divergence: the interpreter would choose coercions at run time where the specification and the compiled path choose them statically (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 3`).
- Risk: the lowest share of derived work; every number is from a run-time survey over all 392 interpreter tests. The risk is direction, not arithmetic: the library's shape moves toward the prelude's, and `Number` loses its catch-alls.

### Route B: drop the rule, instantiate at the call site, enforce the overload sentence

- Checker: rung P's 22-line relaxation, in every analyzer, since only the broad placement reaches `typecase` reachability (`REPORT.md`, "What the placement question looks like"); the sentence, 19 lines in `OverloadingChecker` (`scope-call-site-dispatch.md § 5`). Count 103 to 24 on today's tree (`patents-forest-rule.md § 4`).
- Code generator: 43 lines in `OverloadSet.java`, the arms of a generic dispatcher renamed into the dispatcher's own parameters; `MieDispatchSub` then prints `Marker[Blue]`; the prelude is byte-identical and all 43 generic-overload compiler tests print the same. Not built: generic dotted methods, functional methods, `opr` and `nat` parameters (`scope-call-site-dispatch.md § 3`).
- Library: under the narrower reading (`own`, a functional method's own parameters) 179 api pairs refused, 11 of them errors already, in families whose repair is padding to one parameter list or renaming (juxtaposition 80, `DOT` 48, `CMP` 25, `MIN`/`MAX` 16, range helpers 9, `__cond` 1), plus six other library files; the interpreter accepts the padding. Under the wider reading (`lifted`) 335, refusing the tower's own implementations of `Integral`'s methods, "which the tower cannot survive". Symbolic operators, which the checker never examines, add 329 pairs by text scan (`scope-call-site-dispatch.md § 5`).
- Interpreter: no change for the double membership (it already accepts it) or the shortcut (it already refuses it); on `ScopeArmsX` the two paths already answer differently (`scope-call-site-dispatch.md § 6`).
- Tests: 6 gated compiler tests and 6 gated interpreter tests refused, 3 expected failures too (`scope-call-site-dispatch.md § 5`); `ProbeMIEPick` becomes a gated compile-error test; `Compiled12.invariantInference` goes red under the `skip` variant (`scope-call-site-dispatch.md § 3`).
- Forecloses: the shortcut (`tail`-style specialisation), which the specification never allowed and the interpreter never ran. Keeps `Empty`, the tower, row 330 and C4's bounds as they are.
- Not settled: which reading of "static parameters" a functional method gets, the note recommends neither; whether the sentence covers operators and arities; the specification's own two models of when static arguments are fixed; the dotted-method remainder; the gate not run (`scope-call-site-dispatch.md § 6`).
- Added up here, not in the scope note: the tower's specialised method implementations (`ZZ64`'s `TIMES` beside `Integral[\I\]`'s; `QQ`'s and `Number`'s `MIN`, `MAX`, `MINMAX`) pass the narrower reading and are the inner-level hole the forest probes show, a `ZZ32` reaching `ZZ64`'s body where generic code was promised a `ZZ32` (`patents-forest-rule.md § 3`, "In the library"). The hole is the nesting's, not the rule's, so B keeps it unless it also takes C's completion below (seven declarations plus the derived 40-70 lines) or the wider reading, which flattens by refusal.
- Risk: the smallest measured code and the largest unmeasured reach: 179 is the checker's count of the names it examines, the 329 operator pairs are a text scan, and components and `tests/` were scanned as text only.

### Route C: the patents' forest rule

- Checker: `checkP` lets two instantiations of a self-typed generic exclude only when their arguments are unordered, about 30 lines, in every analyzer, built and measured; `comprises T` on the seven traits in `.fsi` and `.fss` (the shadow accepted the library's bound as the test; under the patents' literal test nothing lifts); the covariant reading of `comprises T`, 3 lines; and a return type rule that checks every self-typed level below a specialisation unless a more specific declaration covers it, 40-70 lines, not built, derived from the probes and from no source (`patents-forest-rule.md § 2, § 4`). Count 103 to 37, the 13 marker errors staying until the markers go.
- Code generator: dispatch made to agree with the checker's static choice under the covariant reading, not sized; and the 43-line call-site fix, still needed on a chain (`patents-forest-rule.md § 3, § 4`).
- Library: the markers dropped (2 declarations); seven inner-level specialisations completed at every level below (`ZZ64`'s `TIMES`; `QQ`'s and `Number`'s `MIN`, `MAX`, `MINMAX`); `Integral comprises I` beside `AnyIntegral comprises { ZZ }` unmeasured (`patents-forest-rule.md § 3, § 6`).
- Interpreter: the probe pair with `comprises T` overflows its overload check's stack; without the specialisation it runs (`patents-forest-rule.md § 3`).
- Tests: all four of rung P's probes behave as under the stock checker; new tests for the forest, the covariant reading and the return rule (`patents-forest-rule.md § 4`).
- Forecloses: `Empty extends List[\T\]` and `Both` stay illegal (`patents-forest-rule.md § 1`). Keeps the tower, row 330, the shortcut and C4's bounds.
- Not settled: the return type rule has no source; whether `comprises T` is read covariantly; which instance a checked call takes on a chain (the compiled checker takes the top, the interpreter and the patents the bottom); the checker-dispatch order mismatch under the covariant reading; symbolic operators still escape the overloading check (`patents-forest-rule.md § 6`; `dispatch-and-route-c.md § 2`).
- Risk: the highest share of derived work. Of five pieces two are built; the soundness rule is ours; no paper published the forest and the checker never implemented it; the team's own comprises-based subtyping attempt overflowed in 2012.

### Hybrids, and the counts that disagree

- The forest for the tower plus the call-site fix, without the overload sentence, is route C as the forest note prices it: the sentence is not among its five pieces, and its overload half is the completion rule (`patents-forest-rule.md`, the routes). The notes hold no cheaper cut of C: dropping the return type rule leaves `ForestGeneric`'s hole open.
- A flat machine-width tower (`ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` as coercing siblings, the specification's own example) with ℤ inside ℚ inside ℝ kept as subtyping would still need the forest rule for the upper chain, since `ZZ` carries `Equality` at `ZZ`, `QQ` and `Number`; its price is A's conversion sites for the fixed widths only plus all of C. No note splits the survey's sites by level, so this hybrid is named here, not priced.
- The counts disagree by tree and by instrument. 93 to 33 (`REPORT.md`) was rung P's relaxation on the pre-L base `d610695c0`; 103 to 24 (`patents-forest-rule.md § 4`) is the same switch on today's tree after rung L's api repairs; 103 to 22 (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 5`) is the flat library under the stock checker, and its two fewer are the `comprises` errors the flat `AnyIntegral` makes well formed; 103 to 37 is the forest. All four are the gate's instrument, which stops the `FortressLibrary` api at its hierarchy stage. The scope note's 203 (`scope-call-site-dispatch.md § 5`) is the zero probe's stack, which repairs that stop so the overloading check reaches the api; it is a deeper instrument, so its 203 to 382 under the sentence cannot be laid beside 22, 24 or 37.

## 4. Weighing, as he asked

- The premise (`POSITIONS.md:80`): the specification "was written in a vacuum early on", "as a wish"; the type group "knew much more about what's feasible"; "when that wish met reality, then the spec must change"; strong weight on "whatever Naden was thinking and where he was driving the design".
- Applied to the dated facts, the premise selects: the rule stays, because it is the group's implemented and published position (2010-2011, Steele among the authors, restated in 2012 and 2019); the overload sentence carries no weight, because it is 2009 text never revised and enforced by neither path; and `Empty extends List[\T\]` and ℤ-inside-ℚ-as-subtyping carry little, because the compiled checker never implemented them. That puts route B outside the premise: its footing is the spec sentence and the interpreter.
- Between A and C the premise's own facts split. For A: Steele's flattening is the group's implemented resolution of this exact conflict in the compiled world (2011-07), and their last published line (POPL 2019) has no self types and no tower. For C: the patents are the latest thing they wrote (2012-08-31, after the flattening, Naden and Steele among the inventors) and they keep the tower; but they are claims, never built, their self-typed dispatch step is commented out in Welterweight, and the checker's one comprises-based attempt overflowed (2012-06-06).
- Where the facts complicate the premise: the interpreter and its library are the group's too, and they kept the nesting and refused the shortcut to the end; the sentence B rests on was never enforced, but neither was the nesting ever checked by the compiled checker; and "where Naden was driving" points two ways on one day, the self-type bound `add[\X <: Ring[X]\]` (a flat tower's idiom) in his write-up and the forest in the patent.
- What the premise does not settle: it ranks texts by date and by whether they were implemented, and the two implemented halves are both the group's, their reconciliation implemented by no one. So between A and C the premise leaves a judgement, not a ranking, and the judgement below is made on what is measured against what is derived.
- The case for A, as its advocate would put it: every peer he named flattened, Steele flattened, the specification's own mechanism between widths is coercion, every number is measured, and no type theory of ours goes into the checker; the count falls furthest; the interpreter gets the mechanism the team left a TODO for; and microGPT's text changes nowhere under remedy (i).
- The case for B: the specification and the interpreter, both theirs, allow the type and refuse the shortcut, and no gated interpreter program uses the shortcut; every static-resolution peer allows the double membership; the code is 22, 43 and 19 lines, all measured, with the prelude and 43 generic tests unchanged; the tower and row 330 stay as decided; the 179-pair repair is padding both paths already accept.
- The case for C: it alone keeps all three things the group built, the rule, the nested tower and the shortcut; it is their last word; the checker half is built and lifts 48 of 61; the completion is seven declarations and the rule 40-70 lines; the markers it cannot lift are read nowhere; the library's shape, the specification's ℤ inside ℚ and row 330 change not at all.

## 5. The recommendation

Route A, keep the rule and flatten the tower, with the interpreter taught coercion (remedy i) rather than the sites converted by hand. The reasoning: it is the one route in which nothing is derived, every number comes from a survey over the whole test corpus, and the checker, the part he has said he cannot judge, is not touched; it is the group's own implemented resolution of this conflict (Steele, 2011-07) and the shape of every high-performance peer he named; under his premise the two things it gives up, ℤ inside ℚ as subtyping and `Empty extends List[\T\]`, are early spec text the compiled checker never implemented; and the shortcut, which the group's late work was built to keep, stays. B is not chosen because its footing is the weakest text and, as measured, it either keeps the tower's inner-level hole or refuses the tower's own methods. C is not chosen because its soundness rule is ours, not theirs, and building it is the type-theory design he has said he does not want to own.

- Cost in the project's units: two rungs, each gated on the full suite (a gate run is 739 s, `microgpt-run-c-handover.md:16`). By batch 3's rate, 1.64 M tokens and about 80 minutes per rung landed (`coordinator/climb-batch-3-cost.md:19`), so about 3.3 M as a two-rung batch; the batch 3.5 estimate for two rungs is 7 to 13 agents and 2 to 4 M (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-3.5.md:191`). The library rung is the larger.
- What he would be committing to: the library's tower takes the prelude's shape for good; ℤ inside ℚ inside ℝ becomes three coercions and a recorded spec deviation; the interpreter chooses coercions at run time, a recorded divergence from the specification's static rule; `Empty extends List[\T\]` stays unsupported on the compiled path; `SUM` and `PROD` are redesigned; the `AnyIntegral` closure's `NOT YET` comment and its five-line accommodation of 2026-09-21 are withdrawn as moot; row 330's rationale is restated on coercion with its decision unchanged; the tripwire test is deleted.
- What stays open and comes back to him: which of the three `SUM`/`PROD` replacements; generic inference over mixed widths (`lo:hi`); the interpreter outputs that change when a wide binding really widens; and the two code-generator defects and the overloading checker's blindness to symbolic operators, which are holes under every route and not in the ledger yet (`dispatch-and-route-c.md § 3`).
- What a no to every route costs: the switch-over stays where rung P left it, 61 of the 103 errors at the tower, the tripwire test standing, no library batch that touches the numbers briefable, and the checker-count stage holding its 103 (`REPORT.md`, "The stop"; `POSITIONS.md:77`).
- The first rung to build: the interpreter coercion rung. It calls the already-lifted `coerce_<trait>` functions at `OverloadedFunction.bestMatch` ("TODO add checks for COERCE"), at the single-closure sites and at the typed bindings, about 150-200 lines in six files, with the keep note's `FlatCall`, `FlatOverload` and `FlatBind` probes as the tests written red first, and no library line changed. Today's nested tower needs no coercion, so the gate stays green on it, and it is the prerequisite the library rung cannot do without (`price-keep-the-rule.md § 3, § 6`).
- If he chooses B, the first rung is the 43-line call-site fix for top-level functions with `MieDispatchSub` and `ScopeArms` as its gated tests, since it is measured, changes no gated output, and B and C both need it (`scope-call-site-dispatch.md § 3`). If he chooses C, the first rung is the measured `checkP` change with `comprises T` on the seven traits and the markers dropped, count declared 24, with the return type rule probed in a shadow before the second rung is briefed (`patents-forest-rule.md § 4`).

## 6. Open questions for him

- Is ℤ inside ℚ inside ℝ64 as subtyping, the reasoning of row 330, something the language must state itself, or is coercion between them acceptable as the specification already has it between machine widths (a yes to subtyping points to C, not A)?
- Does he weigh the patents' forest rule, the group's latest text but never built, above Steele's implemented flattening of 2011 (a yes points to C)?
- Does the judge's reading of "one library, the interpreter's" as forbidding the prelude's tower shape stand, or did the decision settle only which files survive (if it stands, A is out)?
- Is the specialisation shortcut something the one library must keep, or would he give it up, which is what B needs and what, under the wider reading of the sentence, ends in a flattened tower anyway?
- Does he accept the interpreter choosing coercions at run time, a recorded divergence from the specification's static rule, or must the interpreter match the compiled path's static choice, which turns A's first rung into the by-hand conversion of 367 sites?

     5	component mandelbrot_swifty
     6	export Executable
     7	
     8	asciiGradient: String = " .,:;|!([$O0*%#@"
     9	maxIter: ZZ32 = |asciiGradient|
    10	
    11	toAscii(n: ZZ32): Char = asciiGradient[n - 1]
    12	
    13	object ℂ(re: RR64, im: RR64)
    14	  isPotentiallyInSet(): Boolean = ((re re) + (im im)) <= 4.0
    15	  opr +(self, other: ℂ): ℂ = ℂ(re + other.re, im + other.im)
    16	  opr TIMES(self, other: ℂ): ℂ =
    17	    ℂ((re other.re) - (im other.im), (im other.re) + (re other.im))
    18	end
    19	
    20	(* imperative: Swift's repeat/while, emulated *)
    21	imperative(c: ℂ): ZZ32 = do
    22	  var z: ℂ := ℂ(0.0, 0.0)
    23	  var i: ZZ32 := 0
    24	  var go: Boolean := true
    25	  while go do
    26	    z := (z TIMES z) + c
    27	    i := i + 1
    28	    go := z.isPotentiallyInSet() AND (i < maxIter)
    29	  end
    30	  i
    31	end
    32	
    33	(* functional: tail-recursive orbit counter, same escape semantics *)
    34	countOrbit(z0: ℂ, c: ℂ, i: ZZ32): ZZ32 = do
    35	  z = (z0 TIMES z0) + c
    36	  j = i + 1
    37	  if z.isPotentiallyInSet() AND (j < maxIter) then countOrbit(z, c, j) else j end
    38	end
    39	
    40	mandelbrotF(c: ℂ): ZZ32 = countOrbit(ℂ(0.0, 0.0), c, 0)
    41	
    42	(* julia family: closure over the constant, as in the Swift original *)
    43	julia(c: ℂ): ℂ -> ZZ32 = fn z => countOrbit(z, c, 0)

    45	w: ZZ32 = 64
    46	h: ZZ32 = 32
    47	dx: RR64 = 4.0 / 64.0
    48	dy: RR64 = 4.0 / 32.0

    50	renderFractal(renderer: ℂ -> ZZ32): String = do
    51	  var art: String := ""
    52	  var cy: RR64 := -2.0
    53	  for r <- seq(0#h) do
    54	    var row: String := ""
    55	    var cx: RR64 := -2.0

    59	    end

    61	    cy := cy + dy
    62	  end
    63	  art
    64	end

    67	  t0 = nanoTime()
    68	  art = renderFractal(renderer)
    69	  t1 = nanoTime()
    70	  (art, (t1 - t0) / 1000000000.0)
    71	end

    75	  (artF, tF) = timeRender(mandelbrotF)

    78	  println("functional  " || tF || "s")

    83	  println("Douady's rabbit:")

    85	end

1	# Swift versus Fortress: One Mandelbrot, Two Philosophies
     2	
     3	*An explainer built from a real port: [palimondo/MandelbrotSwifty](https://github.com/palimondo/MandelbrotSwifty) translated to canonical Fortress and executed on the revived 2012 reference interpreter.*
     4	
     5	## The program
     6	
     7	Both versions render an ASCII Mandelbrot: a 16-character gradient `" .,:;|!([$O0*%#@"` doubles as the iteration cap, each pixel escapes or survives `z ← z² + c`, and the count indexes the gradient. Identical algorithm, identical output. Everything interesting is in what each language made easy, hard, or free.
     8	
     9	## Defining a complex number
    10	
    11	Swift (2016-era, from the original repo):
    12	
    13	```swift
    14	struct ComplexNumber { let Re: Double; let Im: Double }
    15	typealias ℂ = ComplexNumber
    16	
    17	func + (x: ℂ, y: ℂ) -> ℂ { return ℂ(Re: x.Re + y.Re, Im: x.Im + y.Im) }
    18	func * (x: ℂ, y: ℂ) -> ℂ { ... }
    19	extension ℂ { func isPotentiallyInSet() -> Bool { ... } }
    20	```
    21	
    22	Fortress:
    23	
    24	```fortress
    25	object C(re: RR64, im: RR64) extends MultiplicativeRing[\C\]
    26	  getter one(): C = C(1.0, 0.0)
    27	  opr +(self, other: C): C = C(re + other.re, im + other.im)
    28	  opr -(self): C = C(-re, -im)
    29	  opr TIMES(self, other: C): C =
    30	    C((re other.re) - (im other.im), (im other.re) + (re other.im))
    31	  opr ^(self, other: AnyIntegral): C =
    32	    if other <= 0 then self.one else self (self^(other - 1)) end
    33	end
    34	```
    35	
    36	Surface similarities are real: both allow Unicode identifiers (Swift's `typealias ℂ` vs Fortress naming the type `ℂ` directly), both are value-oriented (Swift `struct` with `let`; Fortress constructor parameters are immutable fields), and both let you define operators. The philosophical split is in the one clause the Swift version has no counterpart for: `extends MultiplicativeRing[\C\]`.
    37	
    38	## The mathematical machinery: what the ring buys you
    39	
    40	`MultiplicativeRing` is a library trait, not compiler magic. Its full text:
    41	
    42	```fortress
    43	trait AdditiveGroup[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\]
    44	    getter zero(): T = self - self
    45	    opr +(self, other: T): T
    46	    opr -(self, other: T): T = self + (-other)
    47	    opr -(self) : T = self.zero - self
    48	end
    49	
    50	trait MultiplicativeRing[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]
    51	        extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], AnyMultiplicativeRing }
    52	    getter one(): T
    53	    opr TIMES(self, other:T): T
    54	    opr juxtaposition(self, other:T): T = self TIMES other
    55	    opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral): T
    56	end
    57	```
    58	
    59	The generic bound `T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]` is F-bounded polymorphism — the same idea as Swift protocols' `Self` requirements, written out longhand. The payoff is the defaults. `C` above defines only what the mathematics requires — identity, addition, negation, multiplication, exponentiation — and inherits the rest:
    60	
    61	- **Juxtaposition** (`z z` means z·z) comes from the trait default `juxtaposition = self TIMES other`.
    62	- **Binary minus** is never written; `w - w` runs the default `self + (-other)` through the hand-written unary minus.
    63	- **`zero`** is a three-default chain: the trait computes it as `self - self`, which calls the default binary minus, which calls the user's unary minus. Verified on the 2012 interpreter: `w.zero` prints `0.0 + 0.0i`.
    64	
    65	Swift can do default implementations too — protocol extensions derive `!=` from `==`, `AdditiveArithmetic` exists since Swift 5 — so the difference is not capability but *organizing principle*. Swift's numeric protocols are pragmatic API bundles designed around what the standard library needs. Fortress's are abstract algebra transcribed: the spec-era slide decks show `Associative⟦T,⊙⟧` and `Commutative⟦T,⊙⟧` carrying `property ∀(a,b,c) ...` law declarations intended for automated checking. (Honest footnote: the `property` machinery never shipped in the implementation — the vision outran the toolchain, a recurring Fortress theme.)
    66	
    67	## Multiplication without an asterisk
    68	
    69	Fortress has no `*` operator. Zero definitions in the entire library — the 2005 design deck says why: "Asterisks are for accountants." Mathematics writes multiplication three ways, so Fortress supports three independent, separately overloadable operators: juxtaposition (`a b`), `·` (DOT), and `×` (TIMES). Juxtaposition is a genuine named operator, `opr juxtaposition`, participating in overload dispatch like anything else — the library overloads it for scalar×vector and matrix×matrix at top level. That is how `3 sin pi x - log x + 5 z^2` parses as mathematics: someone overloaded whitespace.
    70	
    71	Two guardrails make this survivable where FORTRAN's whitespace-blindness (`DO20I=1.125`) was a famous trap:
    72	
    73	1. **Whitespace expresses intent.** `a+b·c+d` and `a + b·c + d` are fine; `a+b · c+d` is rejected — spacing that contradicts precedence is a compile error. (This bit us live: `C(1.0,1.0)^4` is rejected because an argument list may not tightly abut `^`; parenthesizing the base fixes it.)
    74	2. **Nontransitive precedence.** `+` binds tighter than `>`, and `>` tighter than `∨`, but `a + b ∨ c + d` is an error — no precedence is defined between `+` and `∨` at all. With hundreds of operator symbols, only the universally memorized precedences exist; everything else takes parentheses.
    75	
    76	Swift sits at the opposite pole: operators are token sequences with declared global precedence groups, whitespace is (mostly) insignificant, and juxtaposition means nothing. Both are defensible; only one lets you type a polynomial the way you'd write it on a whiteboard.
    77	
    78	## Parallelism for free: monoids and BIG operators
    79	
    80	The deepest difference. The complete Fortress renderer:
    81	
    82	```fortress
    83	art(): String =
    84	  BIG //[r <- 0#32]
    85	    (BIG ||[k <- 0#64] toAscii(mandelbrot(C(-2.0 + k dx, -2.0 + r dy))))
    86	```
    87	
    88	Two nested comprehensions: `BIG ||` concatenates a row of characters, `BIG //` joins rows with newlines. No loop, no mutation, no index arithmetic beyond the coordinate formula — and no requested parallelism, because none needs requesting. Fortress evaluates comprehensions as *reductions over a monoid*: string concatenation is associative, so the runtime is free to split the range, render chunks on different threads via work-stealing, and combine. The slide-deck slogan: reduction operators and comprehensions "are exactly like" each other — `∑` desugars to a generator call with a `SumReduction` object whose entire definition is `empty()` and `join(a,b) = a + b`. Declare the algebraic structure; the evaluation strategy follows.
    89	
    90	The typing that makes this safe is the same trait machinery as above: `∑` is defined (in the library, not the compiler) roughly as
    91	
    92	```fortress
    93	opr SUM[\E, T extends Monoid[\T,+\]\](g: Generator[\E\], body: E -> T): T
    94	```
    95	
    96	so a type earns the right to be summed in parallel by extending `Monoid` — algebra as an API contract.
    97	
    98	The Swift equivalent of the sequential version is easy (`map`/`joined`). The *parallel* version is not: you reach for `DispatchQueue.concurrentPerform` or a `TaskGroup`, manage chunking, and prove to yourself the merge is associative — the language neither knows nor checks. Steele's own comparison slide makes the point against Scala with a comment: the recursive tree walk is marked `⊛ Potentially parallel recursion` in Fortress and `// Sequential` in Scala. Swift stands with Scala here.
    99	
   100	One more free lunch in that snippet: `k dx` multiplies an integer by a float with no cast, because the Fortress numeric tower makes subtyping follow set inclusion — ℤ32 <: ℤ64 <: ℤ <: ℚ <: ℝ64. A 32-bit integer *is* a real number, so mixed arithmetic is ordinary dispatch, not coercion.
   101	
   102	## What Swift took from Fortress
   103	
   104	The influence ran the other way too, and Steele said so. The JuliaCon 2016 deck's closing example of Fortress ideas surviving "by hopping from one language to another" is Swift's optional binding — `if x ← z then f(x) else y end` with `z: Maybe⟦T⟧` — cited by Steele as Fortress syntax living on in `if let`. Good ideas outlive their languages; the language that develops an idea may not be the one that ships it to millions.

326
327 (** Place holder for exclusions of AdditiveGroup **)
328 trait AnyAdditiveGroup end
329
330 (** Additive group making use of +. Must define + and either unary or binary -. **)
331 trait AdditiveGroup[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\] extends AnyAdditiveGroup
332 getter zero(): T = self - self
333 opr +(self, other: T): T
334 opr -(self, other: T): T = self + (-other)
335 opr -(self) : T = self.zero - self
336 end
337
338 (** Place holder for exclusions of MultiplicativeRing **)
339 trait AnyMultiplicativeRing end
340
341 (** Multiplicative ring using TIMES and juxtaposition.
342 Define opr TIMES; juxtaposition is defined in terms of TIMES. **)
343 trait MultiplicativeRing[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]
344 extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], AnyMultiplicativeRing }
345 getter one(): T
346 opr TIMES(self, other:T): T
347 opr juxtaposition(self, other:T): T = self TIMES other
348 (** Exponentiation need only deal with natural exponents. **)
349 opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral): T
350 end
351
352 trait Number
353 extends { StandardPartialOrder[\Number\], StandardMinMax[\Number\],
354 AdditiveGroup[\Number\], MultiplicativeRing[\Number\] }
355 comprises { RR64 }
356 getter zero(): Number = 0.0
357 getter one(): Number = 1.0
358 asFloat(self): RR64
359 opr |self| : Number = |asFloat(self)|
360 opr =(self, b:Number):Boolean = asFloat(self) = asFloat(b)
361 opr =/=(self, b:Number):Boolean = asFloat(self) =/= asFloat(b)
362 opr <(self, b:Number):Boolean = asFloat(self) < asFloat(b)

370 else Unordered
371 end
372 (** In case of NaN, %MIN% and %MAX% return a NaN, otherwise it respects the

437 (** check_star returns Just(its argument) if it is non-NaN, otherwise Nothing. **)

449 that %MAXNUM% and %MIN% form a lattice with NaN at the bottom. **)

451 r = self MIN b

1	(* MicroGptFlat -- microGPT in native Fortress arrays, data designed after Hsu
     2	   (Run C4, the synthesis of rounds two and three: explorations/run-c4/design.md).
     3	   The model only: hyperparameters, the layout table, the four vector
     4	   functions, the step, Adam and the training loop, line for line against
     5	   explorations/apl/reference/hsu-flat/microgpt_concise.dyalog and the formulas
     6	   (the tour: explorations/run-c4/tour.md).  The array vocabulary is FlatArrays,
     7	   the loaders and the corpus FlatData.  Run from explorations/run-c4/src: the
     8	   paths are relative. *)
     9	component MicroGptFlat
    10	export MicroGptFlat
    11	export Executable
    12	import FlatArrays.{...}
    13	import FlatData.{...}
    14	import System.{...}
    15	
    16	(* --------------------------------------------------- hyperparameters ---- *)
    17	(nEmbd, blockSize, nHead, headDim, vocabSize, bosId) = (16, 16, 4, 4, 27, 26)
    18	(epsilon, lr0, beta1, beta2, epsilon_A, nSteps) = (10.0^(-5), 0.01, 0.85, 0.99, 10.0^(-8), 1000)
    19	(corpusPath, weightsDir) = ("../../apl/reference/dzaima/docs.txt", "../../apl/reference/dzaima/w")
    20	
    21	(* ^T on a matrix and on every plane of a rank-3 array, declared here and not
    22	   in the vocabulary because an API cannot declare a postfix operator (row 133) *)
    23	opr (m: Matrix[\RR64,r,c\])^T[\nat r, nat c\]: Matrix[\RR64,c,r\] = transpose(m)
    24	opr (t: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,b,0,c\])^T[\nat a, nat b, nat c\]: Array3[\RR64,0,a,0,c,0,b\] = transpose(t)
    25	
    26	(* -------------------------------------- rmsn, sm and their backward ------ *)
    27	rmsn(x: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): Array[\RR64,ZZ32\] = x / SQRT (epsilon + (x DOT x) / |x|)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Summarise NestProbe counts.  usage: analyze.py <out-dir> <summary-prefix>
Reads <out-dir>/<test>.tsv (count, kind, category, target, leaf, site) written by one walk run
per test, and writes <prefix>-sites.tsv (one row per dependent call site, with the tests that
reach it), <prefix>-methods.tsv (inherited method bodies), <prefix>-tests.tsv (per test) and
prints the summary the note quotes.  Paths are made relative to the repository root."""
import collections, glob, os, re, sys

OUT, PREFIX = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
ROOT = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), *[".."] * 5)) + "/"
rows = []
for f in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(OUT, "*.tsv"))):
    test = os.path.basename(f)[:-4]
    for line in open(f, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"):
        p = line.rstrip("\n").split("\t")
        if len(p) != 6: continue
        n, kind, cat, target, leaf, site = p
        site = site.replace(ROOT, "")
        m = re.match(r"^(.*?):(\d+):", site)
        fn, ln = (m.group(1), int(m.group(2))) if m else ("?", 0)
        rows.append((test, int(n), kind, cat, target, leaf, fn, ln))

******************************************************************************)

component BitTwiddle
export Executable

doit[\I extends Integral[\I\]\](n:I,sz:ZZ64) = do
  n_bar = BITNOT n
  z : I = 0
  z_bar = BITNOT z
  assert((BITNOT z_bar), 0,"not not")
  assert((-1), z_bar,"neg")
  assert((BITNOT n_bar), n,"not")
  assert((n BITAND n_bar), 0,"and 0")
  assert((n BITOR n_bar), z_bar,"or 0")
  assert((n BITAND z_bar), n,"and T")
  assert((n BITOR z_bar), z_bar,"or T")
  assert((n BITAND 0), 0,"and 0'")
  assert((n BITOR 0), n,"or 0'")
  assert((n BITXOR n), 0,"xor self")
  assert((n BITXOR 0), n,"xor 0")
  assert((n BITXOR z_bar), n_bar,"xor T")
  assert((n LSHIFT 1), n+n,"shift sum")
  assert((n LSHIFT 3), 8 n,"shift mul")
  assert((n LSHIFT sz), 0,"shiftL out")
  assert((n RSHIFT 1), (n DIV 2),"shift div2")
  assert((n RSHIFT 3), (n DIV 8),"shift div8")
  assert((n RSHIFT sz), 0,"shiftR out")
  assert((n_bar RSHIFT 1) < 0,"shiftR neg")
  assert(((n RSHIFT 1) LSHIFT 1), (n BITAND (BITNOT 1)),"shiftRL")
  assert((n_bar RSHIFT sz), z_bar,"shiftR out neg")
end

run() = do
  n : ZZ32 = 245
  n' : ZZ64 = 24579235987
  doit(n,32)
  println("ZZ32 OK")
  doit(n',64)
  println("ZZ64 OK")
end

(* flat-tower-sketch.fsi -- price-keep-the-rule.md, item 1.  NOT a compilable api: an excerpt
   of Library/FortressLibrary.fsi (and one line of FortressBuiltin.fsi) rewritten in the shape
   of the compiler prelude (ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:506-1000), so
   that no type is a subtype of two instantiations of one generic.  14 headers change: the 12
   declarations that ADD a second instantiation (all of the 23 with errors except Maybe, whose
   errors go with AnyMaybe's fix, and the 10 objects that only inherit one: Int, Long,
   UnsignedLong, IntLiteral, BigNum, LessThan, GreaterThan, EqualTo, Just, Nothing), plus Number
   and RR64, which give up and take the algebra.  make-flat-lib.py applies exactly these headers to copies for the
   checker count (item 5).  "(was ...)" gives today's header.

   The rules the sketch follows:
   1. No self-typed trait (Equality, StandardPartialOrder, StandardMin/Max/MinMax,
      StandardTotalOrder, Integral, AdditiveGroup, MultiplicativeRing) above a leaf.  The
      algebra sits on the leaves only, as in the prelude; Number carries only the two
      non-generic markers, which keeps every array's `excludes AnyMultiplicativeRing` and
      Array3's `excludes AnyAdditiveGroup` true of every number.
   2. Siblings exclude each other; each leaf `comprises` only its objects.
   3. Widening is a `coerce` on the wider type (the prelude's :514-518, :575-576, :816-817,
      :928-929), plus the integer-to-float coercions the specification describes
      (conversions-coercions.tex:60-66) and the prelude never wrote.
   4. Number keeps no operator: a catch-all such as today's `opr +(self, b:Number): RR64`
      applies without coercion to every mixed call, so a coercion would never be chosen
      (conversions-coercions.tex:454-458: coercion is tried only when no declaration applies
      without it), and its RR64 result breaks the return type rule against a leaf's `+`
      once ZZ32 is no longer below RR64. *)

trait Number                                   (* was: extends { StandardPartialOrder[\Number\],
                                                  StandardMinMax[\Number\], AdditiveGroup[\Number\],
                                                  MultiplicativeRing[\Number\] } comprises { RR64 } *)
        extends { AnyAdditiveGroup, AnyMultiplicativeRing }
    (* the 50 operator and function declarations of today's Number go: the arithmetic and
       comparisons to each leaf (they are there already, on every leaf but RR64, which gets
       its own from the algebra traits), the functions (sin, log, floor, ...) to RR64 alone,
       reached from an integer by RR64's coercions below.  asFloat(self): RR64 stays in the
       component, non-generic. *)
end

trait RR64                                     (* was: extends Number comprises { Float, FloatLiteral, RR32, QQ } *)
        extends { Number, StandardPartialOrder[\RR64\], StandardMinMax[\RR64\],
                  AdditiveGroup[\RR64\], MultiplicativeRing[\RR64\] }
        excludes { QQ, AnyIntegral }
        comprises { Float, FloatLiteral, RR32 }    (* RR32 stays below RR64: it adds no instantiation *)
    coerce(x: QQ)
    coerce(x: ZZ)
    coerce(x: ZZ64)
    coerce(x: ZZ32)
    coerce(x: NN64)
    coerce(x: NN32)
    (* today's RR64 getters, plus Number's functions: sin, cos, ..., floor(self): RR64, ... *)
end

trait QQ                                       (* was: extends { RR64, StandardPartialOrder[\QQ\] }
                                                  comprises { AnyIntegral, ... } *)
        extends { Number, StandardPartialOrder[\QQ\], StandardMinMax[\QQ\],
                  AdditiveGroup[\QQ\], MultiplicativeRing[\QQ\] }
        excludes { AnyIntegral }
        comprises { ... }                      (* the component: comprises { Ratio } *)
    coerce(x: ZZ)
    coerce(x: ZZ64)
    coerce(x: ZZ32)
    coerce(x: NN64)
    coerce(x: NN32)
    (* today's QQ methods unchanged.  An integer is no longer a QQ, so ZZ's `/` returns
       Ratio(a, 1) where it returns `a` today (FortressLibrary.fss:860), and the QQ methods an
       integer inherits today (floor, ceiling, truncate, MINNUM, MAXNUM, isFinite, ...) are
       restated on Integral[\I\]. *)
end

trait AnyIntegral                              (* was: extends { QQ } comprises { ZZ } *)
        extends { Number }
        comprises { ZZ, ZZ64, ZZ32, NN64, NN32 }
    (* now closed and well formed: its immediate subtypes are the five leaves, which extend it
       directly; the family E error at .fsi:409-411 and the NOT YET comment go, and the checker
       accommodation of POSITIONS 2026-09-21 (`isEligibleToExtend`) is no longer needed. *)
end

trait Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]     (* was: extends { StandardTotalOrder[\I\], AnyIntegral } *)
        extends { StandardTotalOrder[\I\], AdditiveGroup[\I\] }
    (* the 23 declarations of today unchanged, plus, generically once for all five leaves,
       what a leaf inherits today from ZZ, QQ, RR64 and Number: numerator, floor, ceiling,
       truncate, isFinite, isNumber, odd, even, ... (the measured list is in the note, § 2). *)
end

Coercion is \emph{not} automatically chained in Fortress, unlike some
other programming languages: even if type \VAR{T} can be coerced to
type \VAR{U} and type \VAR{U} can be coerced to type \VAR{V}, it is
not necessarily the case that type \VAR{T} can be coerced to type
\VAR{V}.  Type \VAR{T} can be coerced to type \VAR{V} only if this
coercion is explicitly defined.

The basic principles behind coercion are (1) a decision by the
designer of a trait \VAR{U} that, in all circumstances where a
functional is to be called, an actual argument of some other type
\VAR{T} may be used to satisfy a parameter of type
\VAR{T}, and (2) a language mechanism for putting this decision into
effect automatically and concisely.

\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Frobboz}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{frob}(\VAR{item}\COLONOP{}X) = 5\)\\
\(  \KWD{coerce}(m\COLONOP\TYP{Matrix}) = \ldots  \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  irrelevant! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
\(\KWD{object} \TYP{Bozo}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Frobboz}\rrbracket(t\COLONOP{}T)  \ldots \KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
then this says nothing about whether the type parameter \VAR{T} of \TYP{Bozo}
has coercions, because coercions are not inherited.  (In fact, we can
make a stronger statement: types named by type parameters \emph{do not have coercions}!)

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Checks explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md against the tree: which standalone
# notes are missing a line, which lines name a file that is gone, which lines
# fall outside the set the index is meant to cover, and which paths named in a
# line's prose no longer resolve. Read-only. Exit 1 if the first two are
# non-empty.
#
# The note set is every *.md under explorations/ except run/experiment trees
# (which document themselves in their own README) and evidence directories.
# Edit the two lists below when the shape of the tree changes.

set -uo pipefail

root=$(cd -- "$(dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
index="$root/explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md"
[ -f "$index" ] || { echo "no INDEX.md at $index" >&2; exit 2; }

# Run/experiment trees: a directory holding one run's sources and evidence.
run_roots='apl|astra|blinded-fable|compile-ladder|run-b|run-b2|run-c|run-c3|run-c4|fortify|ci'
# Generic evidence directory names, at any depth.
evidence_dirs='probes|checks|goldens|figures|evidence|measurements|raw|src|tools|gate|cold-cache|reference|archive|build|article|worker|notes|recovered-reports|_prior|__pycache__|existing-tests|failed|png|regen|tic-regen|tour|pairs|combos'

notes=$(cd "$root" && find explorations -name '*.md' \
  | grep -vE "(^|/)[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+-(probes|pairs)/" \
  | grep -vE "(^|/)($evidence_dirs)/" \
  | grep -vE "^explorations/($run_roots)/" \
  | grep -v '^explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md$' \
  | sort)

# Entry keys: the backticked path at the start of an index bullet.
keys=$(grep -oP '^- `\K[^`]+' "$index" | sort -u)
# Entry keys that are notes (drop the .js/.sh entries from the comparison set).
key_notes=$(printf '%s\n' "$keys" | grep '\.md$' | sort -u)

missing=$(comm -23 <(printf '%s\n' "$notes") <(printf '%s\n' "$key_notes"))
stale=$(printf '%s\n' "$keys" | while read -r p; do
  [ -n "$p" ] && [ ! -e "$root/$p" ] && echo "$p"
done)
outside=$(comm -13 <(printf '%s\n' "$notes") <(printf '%s\n' "$key_notes"))

tracked=$(mktemp); trap 'rm -f "$tracked"' EXIT
(cd "$root" && git ls-files) > "$tracked" 2>/dev/null || : > "$tracked"

# Paths named inside a line's prose (not the entry key) that resolve nowhere.
dangling=$(grep -oP '`\K[^`]{1,120}?\.(md|js|sh|py|fss|fsi|html|tic|svg|csv|tsv|txt|yml)(?=`)' "$index" \
  | grep '/' | grep -v '[[:space:]]' | sort -u | while read -r p; do
    if [ -e "$root/$p" ] || [ -e "$root/explorations/$p" ] \
       || [ -e "$root/explorations/coordinator/$p" ]; then continue; fi
    # last resort: the reference may be relative to a directory deeper in the tree
    grep -q "/$p\$" "$tracked" || echo "$p"
  done)

n() { [ -z "$1" ] && echo 0 || printf '%s\n' "$1" | wc -l | tr -d ' '; }

echo "INDEX.md check — $(cd "$root" && git rev-parse --short HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo 'no git')"
echo "notes in scope: $(n "$notes")   index entries: $(n "$keys")"
echo
echo "== notes missing from INDEX.md ($(n "$missing")) =="
[ -n "$missing" ] && printf '%s\n' "$missing"
echo
echo "== index lines naming a file that does not exist ($(n "$stale")) =="
[ -n "$stale" ] && printf '%s\n' "$stale"
echo
echo "== index lines outside the note set, informational ($(n "$outside")) =="
[ -n "$outside" ] && printf '%s\n' "$outside"
echo
echo "== paths named in a line's prose that resolve nowhere ($(n "$dangling")) =="
[ -n "$dangling" ] && printf '%s\n' "$dangling"

[ -n "$missing" ] || [ -n "$stale" ] && exit 1
exit 0

- `explorations/reviews/library-scalar-extension-review-probes.md`: Two pieces of evidence for the tower-closure decision that review left open, 2026-09-20: the compile path's hierarchy checker run three ways over copies of the interpreter's library and then the interpreter against the repaired copy, plus a comparison of the blinded review with the designing workers' arguments; commands in `library-scalar-extension-review-probes/run-all.sh`.
- `explorations/reviews/multiple-instantiation-exclusion.md`: The ground for Pavol's decision on the designers' "multiple instantiation exclusion" after rung P stopped, gathered 2026-09-22 without deciding: the rule in the OOPSLA 2011 paper's and Naden's 2012 words (and Naden's own note that it conflicts with the numeric tower), where the compiled checker enforces it and where the return type rule relies on it, the interpreter measured (it accepts the type, infers the first-listed instantiation from the run-time value and can then fail at a typed binding, and refuses the specialised overload), the specification's side, the 61 errors at 23 library declarations, the peers, the history (`checkP` 2010-07-26, the nested tower 2008), and routes A (keep; about 13 library declarations and widening the interpreter lacks), B (drop; `checkP` relaxed plus a return-type closure) and C (per-trait); probes and captures in `mie-probes/`.
- `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/dispatch-and-route-c.md`: Two measurements for the choice between routes B(b) and C, 2026-09-22: compiled code fixes a generic's static argument at the call site only when nothing can be dispatched, and a dispatched generic arm takes it from the run-time value (whose RTTI records the last-listed instantiation), so a generic-beside-generic set that both B(a) and B(b) accept type-checks and throws `ClassCastException` (B(b)'s precondition does not hold); route C's overload refusal is a 28-line guard in `satisfiesReturnTypeRule` that refuses 69 pairs in `FortressLibrary.fsi` (54 when limited to returns mentioning the parameter), all the tower's own implementations of the exempted traits' functional methods, plus up to 57 symbolic-operator pairs the compiled overloading checker never examines; two codegen defects found on the way; shadow patch, probes and captures beside it.
- `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/literature.md`: What the field did with the exclusion trade after 2012, searched 2026-09-23 with every claim cited to a URL or DOI: POPL 2019 (Park, Hong, Steele, Ryu) kept the invariant exclusion as an ancestor rule and checks the static return type at dispatch, the option Naden rejected; the in-tree Welterweight draft of 2012 is its precursor; two Oracle patents filed the day of Naden's write-up list a "Self-types meet … must form a forest" restriction that admits the tower's chain inside the rule, never published; Julia avoids the trade by single inheritance and gives up static soundness; X10, Java, Kotlin and Scala forbid double instantiation, C#, F#, Rust and Haskell allow it and resolve statically, Ceylon relaxes only variant parameters and has no overloading; Cecil, C#, Swift and Scala flatten the self-typed algebra; no published resolution of the tower conflict and no necessity proof were found; the sites that blocked the search are listed in its header.
- `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/patents-forest-rule.md`: The "Self-types meet" restriction of the 2012 Oracle patents (US 8,843,887 and 8,898,632), read from USPTO's scans: a generic that comprises exactly its parameter may be instantiated several times by one type if the instantiations are ordered by subtyping ("must form a forest"). A shadow `checkP` implementing it takes the interpreter's library from 103 errors to 37, lifting 48 of the 61 exclusion errors (tower, comparisons, `Maybe`) and keeping the 13 on the `DistributesOver` markers, but only with the library's F-bound read as self-typed. The probes (`mie-probes/forest/`) show that the forest alone does not keep a specialisation at an inner level sound: generic code at the level below gets the specialisation's result (`IncompatibleClassChangeError`). It needs a return type rule over every level below, `comprises T` read covariantly, and dispatch ordered to match; so it is a third route that keeps the rule, the tower and specialisation, at more checker work than dropping the rule.
- `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/spec-sentences-dated.md`: Five specification sentences on trait exclusion, generic self-extension, and overload static parameters, dated by direct blob diff between the earliest reachable git copy (`0f49d8698`, 2009-11-06, Sukyoung Ryu) and HEAD, since `--follow` and path-scoped `git log` are unusable here (repo-internals.md:90-96): four are 2008/2009 text untouched through the type group's 2010-2012 implementation push, including the overloading chapter's "static parameters do not enter into the determination" sentence — early thinking, not a post-hoc rationalization of the multiple-instantiation-exclusion rule; the one passage that did move (the advanced Meet Rule's disambiguating-declaration preamble, copyright-dated 2010) has no recoverable authoring commit, one of the ~146 severed links.
- `explorations/reviews/exclusion-design-brief.md`: A design brief for Pavol's route decision on the compiled checker's multiple instantiation exclusion, written 2026-09-24 on the top tier from the ground note, rung P's stop report and the five `mie-probes/` notes, nothing measured: the decision in plain words; the nine steps of protocol § 6 compressed, with the spec sentences dated and the 2008-2012 history; the three routes priced from the notes (keep the rule and flatten, drop it and instantiate at the call site with the overload sentence enforced, the patents' forest rule) with what each forecloses, leaves unsettled and derives rather than measures, and the disagreeing counts explained by tree and instrument; his premise of 2026-09-23 applied to the dated facts with the best case for each route; a recommendation (route A with interpreter coercion, two gated rungs, the interpreter rung first, and the first rung of each alternative); five open questions.
- `explorations/reviews/nat-checking-plan.md`: A plan for checking `nat` static parameters in the compiler's type checker, answering Pavol's "what was the team's initial idea? How to implement it in the spirit they intended?", starting from the `Not yet implemented` thrown by `STypesUtil.makeInferenceArg` for every `nat`, `int`, `bool`, `dim` and `unit` parameter.

# The flat world for users: C4, the tests and a complex number under route A

## 1. The flat world in five lines

- The flat world is route A. Today every number sits on one chain, `ZZ32 <: ZZ64 <: ZZ <: AnyIntegral <: QQ <: RR64 <: Number` (keep, terms). Under A the links go: `ZZ32` is no longer a `ZZ64`, nor `ZZ64` a `ZZ`, nor an integer a `QQ`, nor `QQ` an `RR64`; the integer types, `QQ` and `RR64` become siblings under `Number`, and `AnyIntegral` stays the integers' common parent (keep § 1; the sketch :69-71).
- Each type keeps its algebra at its own type: `Equality`, the orders and `Integral` on the integers, and `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing` on `QQ` and `RR64`, which today have them only at `Number` (keep § 1; the sketch :39-40, :54-55, :77-78).
- Where a narrower number meets a wider one, a `coerce` declared on the wider type converts it: `ZZ64` from `ZZ32`, `ZZ` from the fixed widths, `QQ` and `RR64` from every integer, `RR64` from `QQ` (keep § 1, "Widening"). It is tried only when no declaration fits without it (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:454-458`), and it does not chain (`:127-132`).
- `Number` stays the type every number belongs to, so `T extends Number` stays valid (keep § 4). It loses its algebra and its 52 declared operators and functions, the catch-alls such as `opr +(self, b: Number): RR64 = asFloat(self) + asFloat(b)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:379`; keep § 1).
- The catch-alls cannot stay beside coercion: they fit every mixed call without coercion, so `x + 1` with `x: ZZ64` would run in floating point, and the compiled checker would refuse their `RR64` result beside each integer's own `+` (keep § 1).

## 2. C4, concretely

The 37 microGPT sites the keep note counts are in `explorations/microgpt.fss`, the scalar-autodiff port, not in C4: the survey ran that one program for 50 of its 250 steps (keep § 4; `keep/nestprobe/showcase-microgpt-summary.txt:1-6`). C4 (`MicroGptFlat.fss`, `FlatArrays.fss`, `FlatData.fss`) was never surveyed. The lines below are C4's, found by reading, each set beside the surveyed `microgpt.fss` record of the same shape (`keep/nestprobe/showcase-microgpt-sites.tsv`).

- `MicroGptFlat.fss:27`, `rmsn`: `x / SQRT (epsilon + (x DOT x) / |x|)`; the same at `:31` and `:32`.
  - Today: a float divided by the vector's length, a `ZZ32` (`FortressLibrary.fss:1773`). `Float`'s own `/` takes only a `Float` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:114`), so `Number`'s catch-all `/` runs (`FortressLibrary.fss:385`), reached because an integer is a `Number`; the mirror of `microgpt.fss:63`.
  - (i): the text stands. `|x|` goes through `RR64`'s `coerce(x: ZZ32)` (the sketch :46), which the interpreter already lifts into a callable `coerce_RR64` (keep § 3), and `RR64`'s own `/` runs.
  - (ii): `(x DOT x) / asFloat(|x|)`.
- `:59` and `:66`: `SQRT (1.0 headDim)`.
  - Today: `1.0 headDim` is the program's own way of saying "this integer as a float". A float literal has no arithmetic of its own (`FortressBuiltin.fss:194-201`), so `Number`'s catch-all juxtaposition runs (`FortressLibrary.fss:383-384`). `microgpt.fss:208`'s `SQRT(hd 1.0)` is the surveyed twin, one of its 7 mixed sites.

  - (ii): the idiom itself goes: `SQRT asFloat(headDim)`.

## 1. The flat world in five lines

- The flat world is route A. Today every number sits on one chain, `ZZ32 <: ZZ64 <: ZZ <: AnyIntegral <: QQ <: RR64 <: Number` (keep, terms). Under A the links go: `ZZ32` is no longer a `ZZ64`, nor `ZZ64` a `ZZ`, nor an integer a `QQ`, nor `QQ` an `RR64`; the integer types, `QQ` and `RR64` become siblings under `Number`, and `AnyIntegral` stays the integers' common parent (keep § 1; the sketch :69-71).

It is tried only when no declaration fits without it (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:454-458`), and it does not chain (`:127-132`).
- `Number` stays the type every number belongs to, so `T extends Number` stays valid (keep § 4). It loses its algebra and its 52 declared operators and functions, the catch-alls such as `opr +(self, b: Number): RR64 = asFloat(self) + asFloat(b)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:379`; keep § 1).

## 4. The complex-number test

What `complex_ring.fss` declares and gets:
- It declares `object C(re: RR64, im: RR64) extends MultiplicativeRing[\C\]` and nothing else (`complex_ring.fss:8`), and writes `one`, `+`, unary `-`, `TIMES` and `^` (`:9-15`).
- From the trait's defaults it gets juxtaposition, `z z` as `z TIMES z` (`FortressLibrary.fss:347`), binary minus as `self + (-other)` (`:334`), and `zero` as `self - self` (`:332`), through `MultiplicativeRing` extending `AdditiveGroup` (`:343-344`). Its run shows them in `w - w` and `w.zero` (`complex_ring.fss:26-27`; `swift-vs-fortress-explainer.md:59-63`; `explorations/README.md:23`).
- The library's `Vector` and `Matrix` get their `+`, `-`, unary `-` and `zero` the same way (`FACTS.md:96`).

Where it comes from: the self-typed algebra traits, not the numeric chain. `C` is not a `Number` and is on no chain, so cutting the chain does not reach it; A keeps these traits and puts them on `RR64` and `QQ` at their own type (the sketch :39-40, :54-55).

The lines of `complex_ring.fss` that change under A: none, by reading.
- `:9`, `:21`, `:24-25` build a `C` only from float literals, which are `RR64` under both towers (keep, terms). `C(2, 0)` would lean on the chain today (`keep/FlatExplicit.walk.txt:4`, `k(3)` for `k(x: RR64)`) and need a coercion or `C(2.0, 0.0)` under A; the file never writes it.
- `:10` and `:13` do float arithmetic on the fields. Where a float literal meets a `Float`, it runs `Number`'s catch-alls today and `RR64`'s own under A, with the same text (keep § 4).
- `:14-15`, `opr ^(self, other: AnyIntegral)`: `i^2` and `(C(1.0, 1.0))^4` pass an integer as an `AnyIntegral`, which every integer still is (the sketch :69-71). Under walk `other <= 0` and `other - 1` run the integer's own methods, as today. No static checker has run this file under either tower.

The Mandelbrot programs are the other half of the memory. Their `C` declares no trait: `mandelbrot_canonical.fss:9-15` writes its own juxtaposition (`:14`), and `mandelbrot_swifty.fss:13-18` has only `+` and `TIMES`. What they took from the tower is `-2.0 + k dx` (`mandelbrot_canonical.fss:31`), an integer from `0#64` times a float with no conversion, which the explainer credits to subtyping: "A 32-bit integer *is* a real number, so mixed arithmetic is ordinary dispatch, not coercion" (`swift-vs-fortress-explainer.md:100`). The body that runs is `Number`'s catch-all `asFloat(self) asFloat(b)` (`FortressLibrary.fss:383-384`). It needs only that an integer is a `Number`, which A keeps, and the catch-all itself, which A removes. That is reading, and the survey records the same shape as `Number.juxtaposition<-ZZ32` at `buffons.fss:28` and `microgpt.fss:86`. Under (i) the line stands and `k` is coerced; under (ii) it becomes `-2.0 + asFloat(k) dx`.

Easier or harder to write a complex type in the flat world:
- The same: the conformance and the operations it gives, above.
- The same under (i) and on the compiled path, more text under (ii): mixing a real with a complex. Today nothing does it for free: the catch-alls want a `Number` on both sides and `C` is not one, so `2 z` finds no declaration. The user writes `opr juxtaposition(a: RR64, z: C): C = C(a z.re, a z.im)`. Today that one declaration takes every integer and rational by the chain; under A it takes them by `RR64`'s coercions, one step each (the sketch :43-48), so it stays one declaration. Under (ii) each integer call writes `2.0 z` or `asFloat(n) z`.
- Harder: a `coerce(x: RR64)` inside `C`, to let `z + 2.0` work, does not carry a `ZZ32` along, since coercion does not chain (`conversions-coercions.tex:127-132`); `C` would need one coercion per number type. The interpreter has no coercion today (`FACTS.md:52`), so this spelling is new either way.
- Easier: a complex type generic in its parts, `Complex[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]`, the specification's style of bound, cannot be made at `RR64` today, since `RR64` fails `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]` (`FACTS.md:99`). Under A it can, at `RR64` and at `QQ` (brief § 2.8; the sketch :39-40, :54-55).

## 5. What a user loses and gains under A, with (i)

Loses:
- **`Number` as a type with arithmetic.** `fn (x: Number): RR64 => x + y` (`generatorTest.fss:28`) runs on any number today through the catch-alls. Under (i) it still runs, since dispatch looks at the values and coercion fills the gap, but no `+` on `Number` exists for a static checker (keep § 1). The library's own instance is `SUM`: its replacement is open, and one option loses the empty sum's `0` (keep § 2c; C4's `matOffset(0)`, § 2).
- **The join of mixed widths.** Where a generic's type is inferred from a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` together, as in `lo:hi`, the flat answer is `AnyIntegral`, and what the interpreter then does was not measured (keep § 3, § 6).
- **A value's identity when it is widened.** `q: QQ = z` keeps the `Int` 7 today and prints `7` (`keep/FlatExplicit.walk.txt:5`); under (i) it holds whatever `QQ`'s coercion builds. The sketch has `ZZ`'s `/` return `Ratio(a, 1)` where it returns `a` today (the sketch :63-64; `FortressLibrary.fss:860`), and a `Ratio` prints as `num/den` (`:600`). Whether such values print differently was not measured.
- **Wrapping outputs.** A wide binding prints the wide result (§ 3), arguably the right one: the keep note recorded the wrap as a defect (`FACTS.md:43`).
- **The same choice on both paths.** Under (i) the interpreter picks a coercion as it runs. The specification and the compiled path pick it when the program is checked, and the specification's own example makes the two call different declarations (keep § 3; `conversions-coercions.tex:567-604`).

Gains:
- **The specification's algebraic bounds work on `RR64`**: `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]` and the ring bound (`FACTS.md:99`; the sketch :39-40), the gain of § 4.
- **The specialisation shortcut stays**: a generic function may keep a special version for one instantiation, `tail(x: List[\ZZ\])` beside `tail[\X\](x: List[\X\])` (brief § 1, § 3 route A).
- **One tower shape on both paths**: the interpreter's library takes the compiler prelude's shape, whose tests already widen by coercion and never by hand (keep § 3; `ProjectFortress/library_tests/AverageTest.fss:108`).
- **Wide means wide**: a `ZZ64` variable holds a 64-bit value (§ 3).
- **Text kept**: under (i) no test text changes by design, and microGPT's changes nowhere (keep § 6; brief § 2.8).

## 6. In five lines

- The free operations of the complex type came from the algebra traits, which A keeps and extends to `RR64`; what came from subtyping (really from `Number`'s catch-alls, reached because every number is a `Number`) is mixed arithmetic with no conversion written, `k dx`, `1.0 headDim`, `1 - beta1`, which A keeps for the user only through coercion, so (i) decides whether the ergonomics survive.
- Read, not run: every line verdict on C4, `complex_ring.fss` and the Mandelbrot programs, the claim that C4's digits stay the same, and the (ii) spellings.
- Measured by the keep note and quoted: the 37 microGPT sites, the 207 test sites and their reasons, the probes' outputs in `keep/*.walk.txt`.
- Counted here from the keep note's table: the 112/8 split of the 120 and the file spreads; the table's three-record cut moves one site between the 29 and the 129.
- Open: the `SUM` replacement, which decides whether C4's text stands; the integer as `self` under coercion; the mixed-width join; how many tests print a value that really widens.

4	
5	## 1. The flat world in five lines
6	
7	- The flat world is route A. Today every number sits on one chain, `ZZ32 <: ZZ64 <: ZZ <: AnyIntegral <: QQ <: RR64 <: Number` (keep, terms). Under A the links go: `ZZ32` is no longer a `ZZ64`, nor `ZZ64` a `ZZ`, nor an integer a `QQ`, nor `QQ` an `RR64`; the integer types, `QQ` and `RR64` become siblings under `Number`, and `AnyIntegral` stays the integers' common parent (keep § 1; the sketch :69-71).
8	- Each type keeps its algebra at its own type: `Equality`, the orders and `Integral` on the integers, and `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing` on `QQ` and `RR64`, which today have them only at `Number` (keep § 1; the sketch :39-40, :54-55, :77-78).
9	- Where a narrower number meets a wider one, a `coerce` declared on the wider type converts it: `ZZ64` from `ZZ32`, `ZZ` from the fixed widths, `QQ` and `RR64` from every integer, `RR64` from `QQ` (keep § 1, "Widening"). It is tried only when no declaration fits without it (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:454-458`), and it does not chain (`:127-132`).
10	- `Number` stays the type every number belongs to, so `T extends Number` stays valid (keep § 4). It loses its algebra and its 52 declared operators and functions, the catch-alls such as `opr +(self, b: Number): RR64 = asFloat(self) + asFloat(b)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:379`; keep § 1).
11	- The catch-alls cannot stay beside coercion: they fit every mixed call without coercion, so `x + 1` with `x: ZZ64` would run in floating point, and the compiled checker would refuse their `RR64` result beside each integer's own `+` (keep § 1).

71	## 4. The complex-number test
72	
73	What `complex_ring.fss` declares and gets:
74	- It declares `object C(re: RR64, im: RR64) extends MultiplicativeRing[\C\]` and nothing else (`complex_ring.fss:8`), and writes `one`, `+`, unary `-`, `TIMES` and `^` (`:9-15`).
75	- From the trait's defaults it gets juxtaposition, `z z` as `z TIMES z` (`FortressLibrary.fss:347`), binary minus as `self + (-other)` (`:334`), and `zero` as `self - self` (`:332`), through `MultiplicativeRing` extending `AdditiveGroup` (`:343-344`). Its run shows them in `w - w` and `w.zero` (`complex_ring.fss:26-27`; `swift-vs-fortress-explainer.md:59-63`; `explorations/README.md:23`).
76	- The library's `Vector` and `Matrix` get their `+`, `-`, unary `-` and `zero` the same way (`coordinator/FACTS.md:96`).
77	
78	Where it comes from: the self-typed algebra traits, not the numeric chain. `C` is not a `Number` and is on no chain, so cutting the chain does not reach it; A keeps these traits and puts them on `RR64` and `QQ` at their own type (the sketch :39-40, :54-55).
79

81	- `:9`, `:21`, `:24-25` build a `C` only from float literals, which are `RR64` under both towers (keep, terms). `C(2, 0)` would lean on the chain today (`keep/FlatExplicit.walk.txt:4`, `k(3)` for `k(x: RR64)`) and need a coercion or `C(2.0, 0.0)` under A; the file never writes it.

84	
85	The Mandelbrot programs are the other half of the memory. Their `C` declares no trait: `mandelbrot_canonical.fss:9-15` writes its own juxtaposition (`:14`), and `mandelbrot_swifty.fss:13-18` has only `+` and `TIMES`. What they took from the tower is `-2.0 + k dx` (`mandelbrot_canonical.fss:31`), an integer from `0#64` times a float with no conversion, which the explainer credits to subtyping: "A 32-bit integer *is* a real number, so mixed arithmetic is ordinary dispatch, not coercion" (`swift-vs-fortress-explainer.md:100`). 88	- The same: the conformance and the operations it gives, above.
89	- The same under (i) and on the compiled path, more text under (ii): mixing a real with a complex. Today nothing does it for free: the catch-alls want a `Number` on both sides and `C` is not one, so `2 z` finds no declaration. The user writes `opr juxtaposition(a: RR64, z: C): C = C(a z.re, a z.im)`. Today that one declaration takes every integer and rational by the chain; under A it takes them by `RR64`'s coercions, one step each (the sketch :43-48), so it stays one declaration. Under (ii) each integer call writes `2.0 z` or `asFloat(n) z`.
90	- Harder: a `coerce(x: RR64)` inside `C`, to let `z + 2.0` work, does not carry a `ZZ32` along, since coercion does not chain (`conversions-coercions.tex:127-132`); `C` would need one coercion per number type. The interpreter has no coercion today (`coordinator/FACTS.md:52`), so this spelling is new either way.
91	- Easier: a complex type generic in its parts, `Complex[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]`, the specification's style of bound, cannot be made at `RR64` today, since `RR64` fails `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]` (`coordinator/FACTS.md:99`). Under A it can, at `RR64` and at `QQ` (brief § 2.8; the sketch :39-40, :54-55).
92	
93	## 5. What a user loses and gains under A, with (i)
94	
95	Loses:
96	- **`Number` as a type with arithmetic.** `fn (x: Number): RR64 => x + y` (`generatorTest.fss:28`) runs on any number today through the catch-alls. Under (i) it still runs, since dispatch looks at the values and coercion fills the gap, but no `+` on `Number` exists for a static checker (keep § 1). The library's own instance is `SUM`: its replacement is open, and one option loses the empty sum's `0` (keep § 2c; C4's `matOffset(0)`, § 2).
97	- **The join of mixed widths.** Where a generic's type is inferred from a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` together, as in `lo:hi`, the flat answer is `AnyIntegral`, and what the interpreter then does was not measured (keep § 3, § 6).
98	- **A value's identity when it is widened.** `q: QQ = z` keeps the `Int` 7 today and prints `7` (`keep/FlatExplicit.walk.txt:5`); under (i) it holds whatever `QQ`'s coercion builds. The sketch has `ZZ`'s `/` return `Ratio(a, 1)` where it returns `a` today (the sketch :63-64; `FortressLibrary.fss:860`), and a `Ratio` prints as `num/den` (`:600`). Whether such values print differently was not measured.
99	- **Wrapping outputs.** A wide binding prints the wide result (§ 3), arguably the right one: the keep note recorded the wrap as a defect (`coordinator/FACTS.md:43`).
100	- **The same choice on both paths.** Under (i) the interpreter picks a coercion as it runs. The specification and the compiled path pick it when the program is checked, and the specification's own example makes the two call different declarations (keep § 3; `conversions-coercions.tex:567-604`).
101	
102	Gains:
103	- **The specification's algebraic bounds work on `RR64`**: `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]` and the ring bound (`coordinator/FACTS.md:99`; the sketch :39-40), the gain of § 4.
104	- **The specialisation shortcut stays**: a generic function may keep a special version for one instantiation, `tail(x: List[\ZZ\])` beside `tail[\X\](x: List[\X\])` (brief § 1, § 3 route A).
105	- **One tower shape on both paths**: the interpreter's library takes the compiler prelude's shape, whose tests already widen by coercion and never by hand (keep § 3; `ProjectFortress/library_tests/AverageTest.fss:108`).
106	- **Wide means wide**: a `ZZ64` variable holds a 64-bit value (§ 3).
107	- **Text kept**: under (i) no test text changes by design, and microGPT's changes nowhere (keep § 6; brief § 4).
108

110	
111	- The free operations of the complex type came from the algebra traits, which A keeps and extends to `RR64`; what came from subtyping (really from `Number`'s catch-alls, reached because every number is a `Number`) is mixed arithmetic with no conversion written, `k dx`, `1.0 headDim`, `1 - beta1`, which A keeps for the user only through coercion, so (i) decides whether the ergonomics survive.

114	- Counted here from the keep note's table: the 112/8 split of the 120 and the file spreads; the table's three-record cut moves one site between the 29 and the 129.
115	- Open: the `SUM` replacement, which decides whether C4's text stands; the integer as `self` under coercion; the mixed-width join; how many tests print a value that really widens.

I committed the note and its INDEX line as `2e75daee4`. It is on `main` in the main tree, not pushed. The commit touches only the two files: `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/flat-world-for-users.md` (115 lines) and `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md` (one line). `check-index.sh` reports 0 missing and 0 stale. The note shows up under "outside the note set, informational", the same as the other `mie-probes/` notes.

**A premise to correct before this reaches Pavol:** the keep note's 37 microGPT sites are in `explorations/microgpt.fss`, the scalar-autodiff port, not in C4. C4 was never surveyed. The note finds C4's own dependent lines by reading and puts each beside the surveyed `microgpt.fss` record of the same shape where one exists.

**Section 4 in two sentences:** The complex type's free operations (`zero`, binary minus, `z z`) come from `MultiplicativeRing` and `AdditiveGroup`, the algebra traits A keeps and extends to `RR64`, so no line of `complex_ring.fss` changes (by reading). The Mandelbrot's mixed arithmetic, `k dx`, comes from `Number`'s catch-all juxtaposition, which A removes; under A it works through coercion, or through `asFloat(k)` if sites are converted by hand. One `opr juxtaposition(a: RR64, z: C)` stays a single declaration under coercion, and a generic `Complex[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]` becomes possible at `RR64`, which today's tower does not allow.

**C4 verdict:** with the interpreter taught coercion, C4's text should not change, but only if the replacement for the library's `SUM` keeps an identity. The printed losses should be the same digits, by reading, not by a run.

**Most concrete loss:** `matOffset(0) = SUM[j <- 0#0] matCount(j)` (`MicroGptFlat.fss:43`) is 0 today only because `SumReduction`'s "Hack to permit any Number" gives the sum an identity. Under A that hack goes, and one of the three replacements the keep note leaves open has no value for an empty sum.

**Also found:** `longPrim.fss:20-21` declares `a:ZZ64 = 0` but today checks the 32-bit bounds, because `a` holds an `Int`.
